63: // diff compares two multi-line strings and returns a helpful comment
64: func diff(got, want string) string {
65: 	g := strings.Split(got, "\n")
66: 	w := strings.Split(want, "\n")
67: 	for i := 0; ; i++ {
68: 		switch {
69: 		case i < len(g) && i < len(w):
70: 			if g[i] == w[i] {
71: 				continue
72: 			}
73: 			return fmt.Sprintf("-- first difference in line %d:\n"+
74: 				"-- got : %q\n-- want: %q\n", i+1, g[i], w[i])
75: 		case i < len(g):
76: 			return fmt.Sprintf("-- got %d extra lines after line %d:\n"+
77: 				"-- first extra line: %q\n", len(g)-len(w), i, g[i])
78: 		case i < len(w):
79: 			return fmt.Sprintf("-- got %d correct lines, want %d more lines:\n"+
80: 				"-- want next: %q\n", i, len(w)-i, w[i])
81: 		default:
82: 			return "no differences found"
83: 		}
84: 	}
85: }

This is the classic food-chain exercise. Implement it algorithmically.

Approach:
- Animals: fly, spider, bird, cat, dog, goat, cow, horse (indices 0–7).
- Each animal has a comment line (except for the fly and the horse):
  - spider: "It wriggled and jiggled and tickled inside her."
  - bird: "How absurd to swallow a bird!"
  - cat: "Imagine that, to swallow a cat!"
  - dog: "What a hog, to swallow a dog!"
  - goat: "Just opened her throat and swallowed a goat!"
  - cow: "I don't know how she swallowed a cow!"
  - horse: "She's dead, of course!"
- Verse v (1-based): first line "I know an old lady who swallowed a %s.", then the comment. If the animal is the horse, done. Otherwise, for each animal below it (from v-1 down to 1): "She swallowed the %s to catch the %s[.]", and for the spider, append " that wriggled and jiggled and tickled inside her." Then the final line "I don't know why she swallowed the fly. Perhaps she'll die."

Verses(start, end): join the verses with "\n\n". Song(): Verses(1, 8).

- **`Verse(v)`** — assembles lines for verse `v`: the opening line, the animal's comment (skipped for the fly), the cumulative "She swallowed the X to catch the Y" chain walking back down the food chain (with the spider's wriggling clause), and the closing "Perhaps she'll die" line (omitted for the horse).
